inv.fact_check_detail: Holds: 421M total (ModernBERT-large 395M backbone + decision head trained from scratch), Apache 2.0, non-autoregressive choice/score/noul in one forward pass, base zero-shot typed-decisions accuracy 0.362 vs majority baseline 0.461 (random 0.318); fine-tuned checkpoint 0.766. NOT found on the HF card: the '~110 ms on a 56-core Mac Pro CPU' figure (card gives 39.5 ms/question on a Tesla T4 for English, 193-464 ms for a preloaded Router on CPU, 4000 tokens ~1.7 s on Apple GPU) and a README determinism warning about batch shape / CPU fast paths (card and receptron README give no determinism/batch-invariance warning; the closest are 'pin the revision for reproducibility' and JS/Python float formatting differences). Treat those two as unverified; the conclusion does not depend on them, since weights are float and ONNX/WASM numerics are not guaranteed bit-stable across hardware anyway. Also omitted: card says the model ships over-confident (ECE 0.466 before refit), act_probability has no usable signal, and 'choice' degrades past ~20 options (6 in the browser path).
inv.browser_route: Exists but not as 'laya-ts'. @receptron/laya (npm, MIT code) is Node/TypeScript ONNX Runtime, ~1.7 GB fp32 weights, ~2 GB RAM, no browser claim. jev-web (npm) runs Laya in the browser (WebGPU else WASM, user-supplied module Worker, optional transformers.js peer dep): two-file q8 ONNX (encoder+head), ~520 MB, head batch size 1, choice max 6 options, English, 512-token seq, state capped at 256 tokens. Unofficial HF ONNX exports (e.g. wexare/laya-onnx, fp16 ~900 MB, reports browser memory exhaustion; q8 variants exist). So it is browser-runnable in a worker, but at roughly 520 MB download and WASM-CPU latency on a 2019 i7 that nobody has published.
inv.rec_verdict: Endorse the runtime rejection and the authoring-time-only advisory tier, with two amendments.
inv.amended: (1) Correct the claim text: replace the 110 ms Mac Pro and README determinism warning with the sourced facts (T4 39.5 ms; CPU Router 193-464 ms; no vendor determinism guarantee; pin revision) or mark them unverified. (2) The reason to reject runtime is not size or latency alone but: base model is below the majority-class baseline zero-shot and only beats it after domain fine-tuning (so it needs Uplift-specific training data we would have to build), it is over-confident, float inference breaks the bit-exact replay/save contract, and 520 MB of worker memory competes with the P2 SLM tier. Park it as a measured spike, not a closed door: if the P2 timing spike shows spare headroom, a fine-tuned small classifier could serve as a non-authoritative suggestion for pooled-line selection, with its answer frozen into the save when shown (same rule as TextSourcePort).
inv.note: Owner's interest in a JEV-style model is answered correctly: its niche is typed classification of messy text state, which Uplift does not have at runtime because there is no free-text input and the state is already structured.

inv.amended: Add: specify that noisy-OR assumes independent parents, so corroboration through the same channel or from one origin must be collapsed (key parents by origin Act/channel, take max within a group before combining) or echoes will inflate confidence; spoof is a separate negative term (e.g. confidence * (1 - spoofProb)), not a noisy-OR parent. Use a fixed denominator (e.g. 0..1000 or 0..65535) with table-driven combine (1-(1-a)(1-b) in integer, round half down) so it is bit-stable and commutative/associative-testable; contract test order-independence.
inv.note: Noisy-OR is the standard cheap belief combiner (Pearl; used in BN2O, Bayesian trust nets), is deterministic in integers, and is explainable ('three independent reports'). Good fit for P4 inference trails.

inv.amended: Qualify: decide per tier. Only Tier 1/rival actors need belief-reading utilities; Tier 2/3 can read ground truth through a perception filter. Keep the outcome table small and make each consideration declare which Observation kinds it reads, so the 'omniscient read' of world state is caught by a lint/contract test (consideration functions receive a BeliefView, not WorldState). Add noise-free uncertainty handling: when belief confidence is below a threshold, the option is 'investigate/wait' rather than a best-guess action, which also gives readable NPC behaviour for P4.
inv.note: Making utility terms consume the agent's own beliefs is the standard fix (imperfect-information utility AI, cf. Dave Mark's infinite axis utility, blackboard-per-agent perception in Thief/F.E.A.R.-style sensing). State machines for rival agendas is sound; HTN only on demand is right.

inv.amended: Small amend: banding the hazard to qualitative odds should use hysteresis or fixed band edges evaluated once per watch to avoid flicker, and the advisor's odds must be computed from what the Ship Mind has observed (INV-C principle), not ground truth, with an error term for advisor 'temper'. Counted-CPT Bayes net from self-play is a reasonable later step; keep it as data with a rules hash.
inv.note: Closed-form first is right; it is inspectable and gives the P4 signposting without a learned model.

inv.amended: Add that fitted keys must be tied to the content/rules hash so a rule change invalidates them loudly rather than silently drifting.
inv.note: Offline fitting and search with committed data is the dominant practice for deterministic games (balance tuning, Monte Carlo difficulty curves). The most underrated use here: offline self-play to find degenerate strategies.

inv.amended: Keep rejection of PPL/junction-tree and JEPA at runtime. Soften 'learned nets give no player-visible gain': say 'no gain over symbolic belief-driven decisions for the decisions in the current design; revisit if a decision class appears that depends on unstructured text'. Exact inference on small fixed-structure networks (under ~20 binary nodes, enumerated in integers) is bit-stable and cheap, so 'exact inference cost depends on author structure' is a reason for a node cap, not a rejection; leave the door open for a capped exact-inference node type behind the same Observation contract.
inv.note: Rejection is fair; wording is slightly too absolute given P5.

smaller_models: Yes, but none changes the verdict. sdmlai/nano-jev is reported (search result only, card not fetched) as a 33.4M MiniLM cross-encoder typed-decision model for RAG, with a 22.7M v0.1 variant: this is the only sub-100M candidate found, unaffiliated, and aimed at RAG routing, so its quality on game-state decisions is unknown and unverified. The better-known NanoJev (C-Tianyu/NanoJev, MIT) is 0.6B on Qwen3-0.6B, larger than Laya's neighbour class, not small. Kev is 0.8B/4B/9B on Qwen3.5 (autoregressive, Jev API compatible). Nimble (Bespoke Labs) is Qwen3.5-9B + LoRA. I found nothing on 'Clef-flash' and make no claim about it. All of these are very new and described by secondary sources (DataCamp, pinggy); none has primary evidence of deterministic cross-platform output or of Uplift-type structured-state performance. Even a 20-30M model would need Uplift-specific fine-tuning data, so the real cost is data, not size; the symbolic route (INV-B/C/D) stays the right default, with a small fine-tuned classifier as a possible later spike for pooled-line selection.
